title: I tried eating 30 plants a week. It was surprisingly easy
content:
In the end, I overshot my target and ate a grand total of 51 plants.
Over the last two years, a new health goal has been growing in popularity. First there was 10,000 steps, then five a day . Now we're being encouraged to eat 30 plants per week.
The trend is based on a 2018 study . It found that people who reported eating at least 30 plants per week tended to have more biodiverse gut microbiomes compared to those who ate fewer than ten. Subsequent studies have found that changing your diet to incorporate this much flora each week can improve your microbiome .
This has many well-known benefits such as reducing inflammation and helping us to live healthier, longer lives .
However, when my editor suggested I give the 30-plants trend a go, it initially sounded extremely intimidating and perhaps impossible. I imagined preparing complicated salads for every meal and struggling with the vast quantities of fibre I'd be consuming. But one week on from my experiment, I can report that it was remarkably easy. So easy, in fact, that I accidentally overshot my goal and ended up eating 51 plants in total. Here's how.
First up, you don’t necessarily need 30 as your goal.
Rob Knight, director of the Center for Microbiome Innovation, at the University of California, San Diego, led the research which began the 30-plant trend. He says the number 30 is somewhat arbitrary, especially as there weren't many participants who ate over 30 plants per week in his study. Those who eat 25 or even 20 may also experience similar health benefits, he says.
Those who started with a low number of different plants saw the biggest effect. "If you're already eating a moderate number of plants, the effect is not going to be as large by adding more."
As it has grown in popularity, the goal of eating 30 plants has been gamified. Each additional plant earns you a " plant point ".
There are six main categories of food we can include, which are:
• Fruits
• Vegetables
• Whole grains
• Legumes (beans and pulses)
• Nuts and seeds
• Herbs and spices
Tea, coffee and chocolate count too. All contain compounds, such as antioxidants, which can benefit our health.
The fact that spices are included surprised me. Research shows that adding a mix of spices to everyday meals can result in measurable improvements in gut microbes in as little as 48 hours, explains Federica Amati, a nutrition scientist at Imperial College, London.
Some sources suggest that herbs, spices, tea and coffee should count as a quarter of a point each.
Small changes can quickly affect our "microbe ecosystem" says Amati, but to make this meaningful, we need continued plant diversity.

title: What to know about Pope Leo’s planned lung nodule surgery
content: Pope Leo XIV is scheduled to have an operation this week to remove “a localized nodule” in his lung that was “detected at a very early stage.” It is the first medical event of his 17-month papacy. The Vatican said he will be admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Tuesday and predicted a weeklong hospitalization to recover. Here is what is known: A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (about 1.2 inches) across. It is sometimes detected on a CT scan performed to investigate another problem, such as trauma or a lung infection, according to the American Cancer Society. Experts say the nodule could be benign or malignant and that prompt evaluation is important. If the nodule is cancerous and removed at an early stage, the prognosis is “excellent,” and surgery alone may be sufficient treatment, said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Leo, 71, is considered otherwise healthy and physically fit, both positive factors for his recovery. He said the nodule was discovered during “recent medical tests,” and the Vatican said Monday that no particular health issue prompted the check-up, describing it as “routine.” The Vatican said Leo will undergo surgery in the first days of this week, with a week of recovery expected. Oncologists who aren’t treating him said patients can often be discharged after just a few days, to recover further at home. The exact date of surgery wasn’t released, but Leo had a full slate of audiences and appointments Monday morning and afternoon. The pope will be treated at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, formally known as the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic, a nonprofit Catholic teaching hospital that is part of the Catholic Sacred Heart University. The facility has a special apartment set up for pontiffs on the 10th floor that includes a private chapel. Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was treated there before his May 2025 death during a long illness prompted by a respiratory crisis. St. John Paul II spent so much time at Gemelli that he called it “Vatican III,” after the Vatican itself and the papal summer residence at Castel Gandolfo. Leo has several activities scheduled this week, but the Vatican on Monday canceled all his audiences through October 20. Leo also has a major trip planned November 6 through 17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru . It is unclear whether the surgery and recovery will affect the ambitious itinerary, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and significant altitude changes in Peru. Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he still planned to make the trip. The Vatican has no specific rules governing who takes over if a pope becomes totally incapacitated. Even while unconscious during surgery, Leo remains pope and retains his authority. Pope Francis remained in charge throughout his lengthy hospitalizations, as did St. John Paul II before him. Both made appointments and issued laws and statements from the hospital. A team of officials already handles day-to-day Vatican operations. Medical advances and popes’ longer lifespans, however, have highlighted this gap in church law and prompted calls for the Vatican to prepare for a pope becoming too ill or incapacitated to govern. Two days before revealing his planned surgery, Leo confirmed one significant appointment . On Friday, he approved Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle as the new dean of the College of Cardinals. Tagle, 69, replaces Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re, 92, whose term Francis extended in the weeks before his death. Tagle was designated at the last minute to stand in for Leo at Wednesday’s Mass to close out a conference on family ministry. The dean plays a significant role in a papal transition . He presides over the previous pope’s funeral and helps lead the cardinals’ closed-door meetings before the conclave to discuss the church’s future needs. If he is under 80 when the conclave begins, he also presides over the secret election of a new pope in the Sistine Chapel. The Vatican released a letter Leo wrote to Re on Sunday — the day of his announcement — thanking him for his lifelong service to the church. He noted in particular the role that Re played in the recent papal transition, when he celebrated Francis’ funeral. “I do not think I am mistaken in saying that you, Your Eminence, have been and remain one of the Holy See’s best-known and most esteemed servants,” Leo wrote.

title: 5 parenting tips that work just as well on adults
content: Parenting requires a lot of learning on the job. Raising a 7-year-old, I’ve benefited enormously from the wisdom of teachers, psychologists and other caregivers who have taught me ways to navigate a minefield of tantrums and meltdowns. The more I learn about how to help a little kid through big feelings, the more I realize I need these strategies as much as my son does. Adults often get so wrapped up in the demands of everyday life that we don’t recognize when we’re struggling emotionally, Dr. Jessi Gold, chief wellness officer for the University of Tennessee System and associate professor of psychiatry at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences in Memphis, told me. “We are really focused on the task, not the person doing the task.” Parents teach their kids that their feelings are valid and treat them with compassion, she added, “but we don’t do that to ourselves.” So I’ve started stealing these parenting tricks for myself — and you don’t need to be a parent to make them work for you. A time-out is usually used as punishment, but I submit it can also be a gift you give yourself. When I am feeling overwhelmed — usually because my kid is asking more of me than I can deliver in the moment — sometimes the only way to keep from yelling, “Could everyone just shut up?!” is to remove myself from the situation. I send myself to my room. It’s a “preemptive time-out,” Gold told me. Stepping away from the thing that’s causing the extreme stress or emotion gives you a chance to cool down before saying something you might regret, she said. When I can’t physically escape, saying something like, “I need a minute,” buys me time to collect myself. I stole this one from a preschool handout intended to help pint-size pupils manage their outsize reactions. Young kids tend to respond to spilled milk-level challenges with DEFCON 1-level intensity. It wasn’t until recently that I realized I do the same thing. Maybe I don’t scream and cry and throw myself on the floor, but in my head I’m freaking out. I am inclined to sweat the small stuff, make mountains out of molehills, and let the perfect be the enemy of the good. I will obsess and ruminate and beat myself up for minuscule mistakes. Or spend a disproportionate amount of time and energy weighing a low-stakes decision. Now I try to channel the wisdom of a preschool teacher and ask myself: Is this a big or little problem? If it’s a little one, I can address it quickly or maybe not, but either way I stop letting it rent so much space in my head and push myself to move on. It is hard for a kid to switch from one thing to the next, whether it’s ending playtime to have dinner or putting on shoes to go outside. Transitioning from one activity to another commonly triggers tantrums, according to the Child Mind Institute , a mental health nonprofit. One way to forestall that is to offer a preparatory countdown. It can be something like: “Five more minutes of playing, then we’re leaving the park.” We give kids structured schedules to make their day more predictable and make it clear what’s expected of them. We could give ourselves the same courtesy, Gold said. I’ve recently learned (with the help of a therapist who specializes in ADHD) that I need a countdown clock of my own. I easily lose track of time, especially when I am focused on something, such as writing this article. I’ll know, for example, that I need to leave work in an hour. Then I will look up from my screen to find that 75 minutes have passed. Experts call this “ time blindness .” Now I give myself a five- to 15-minute warning (in the form of a calendar alert or phone alarm) before I need to wrap up what I’m doing. It’s so simple and so profoundly helpful . There are several ways that slow, deep breathing can help diffuse stress . It can ratchet down the infamous fight-or-flight response, slow a racing heart, stabilize blood pressure, and stimulate the vagus nerve to trigger the part of your nervous system that makes you feel relaxed. Whenever my son gets worked up, my go-to move is to tell him to take three deep breaths and count to five. You fell down and skinned your knee? Oh no, let’s take three deep breaths. You’re on the verge of a tantrum because I turned off the TV? Three deep breaths. Nervous walking into a new classroom? I hear you, dude: three deep breaths. I’ll slowly inhale through my nose and exhale through my mouth to show him what I want him to do. Secretly, I am also trying not to lose it. There is a reason that parents of young children travel with snacks : We know that a hangry kid is a recipe for disaster. Yet I’ll run for hours on a cup of coffee during a busy day, then wonder why I feel unfocused, bedraggled and downright grouchy. It could be burnout or a migraine or the patriarchy — or I might just be dehydrated. “Our physical health is integrated very much into our mental health,” Gold said. If you don’t eat, drink or sleep, “you’re going to be meaner and crankier, and you’re going to cry when you don’t expect it, just like your kids would.” It is amazing what a glass of water and a handful of pistachios can do. If only we all had a mom with a purse full of snacks to help us through the day.
